results.title: Create a Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Define a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework that conceptually describes how systemic risks are assessed, accepted, and mitigated across the model lifecycle.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define, at a conceptual and descriptive level, the key elements required for systemic risk management under the Safety and Security Chapter (including trigger points, risk acceptance logic, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, and update processes)?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly describes its purpose as managing systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
The framework outlines how systemic risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated at a high level.
The framework describes trigger points at which additional evaluations or assessments would occur during the model lifecycle.
The framework defines how systemic risk acceptability is determined, including the use of risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
The framework describes, at a high level, expected categories or types of safety and security mitigations associated with different risk levels.
The framework explains how responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation is allocated within the organization.
The framework describes whether and how input from external actors may influence risk-related decisions.
The framework describes how and under what conditions the framework itself would be reviewed or updated.
results.reasoning: All 8 indicators of Expected Evidence are addressed at a high level (purpose, lifecycle risk management, trigger mechanisms via ongoing monitoring/periodic reviews, accountability, risk tolerance/prioritization, external input, and framework update processes). However, explicit operational trigger criteria beyond periodic reviews, fully defined risk-tiered mitigation categories, and quantified risk-acceptance thresholds are not specified, leaving material gaps that prevent full compliance.

External input and broad stakeholder engagement across the lifecycle

decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit, operational trigger criteria beyond periodic reviews (e.g., event-based or threshold-driven triggers for additional risk assessments)
Defined, risk-tiered mitigation categories mapped to specific systemic risk levels
Quantified risk acceptance criteria or tiers (clear thresholds for acceptability)

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

selected_evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The
first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms,
roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be effective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate
incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at
senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addition, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF
may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and
resources.

results.title: Implement the Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework is intended to be applied across the entire model lifecycle, including continuous systemic risk assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how its systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes are intended to be applied across the model lifecycle, including continuous assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident consideration, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.
The framework explains how lighter-touch evaluations are conducted at predefined trigger points (e.g. based on time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
The framework explains how information about serious incidents or near misses is taken into account within the risk assessment process.

The framework describes how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs can lead to deeper analysis or escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
The framework outlines the sequence or structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
results.reasoning: The text supports lifecycle-spanning governance and ongoing risk management (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and notes incident-informed risk treatment, addressing indicator 1. However, it lacks explicit trigger-point lightweight evaluations, post-market monitoring specifics, a defined escalation pathway to a full systemic risk assessment, and a clear stepwise sequence for the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (indicators 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6). These missing operational details cannot be fully offset by thematic alignment.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle-spanning governance and risk management (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Regular monitoring and incident-informed risk treatment within the MANAGE function
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit trigger-point lightweight evaluations at predefined points (e.g., time, development stage, compute usage, access, or affordances).
Specific post-market monitoring mechanisms and how post-market data feed into ongoing systemic risk assessment.
A clear escalation pathway to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process, including roles, responsibilities, authorities, and timelines.
An explicit, stepwise sequence/structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
Explicit integration of incident inputs (serious incidents and near-misses) into the risk assessment process and how they influence trigger points or escalation.

alignment_findings.alignment_summary: It aligns with conceptual requirements for lifecycle-wide governance and continuous risk management, but lacks explicit details on trigger points, post-market monitoring specifics, and a defined escalation pathway to a full systemic risk assessment.

5.2
Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.
Page 24
NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

results.title: Framework updates
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
results.reasoning: Found indicators: 5 (updates to stay state-of-the-art) and 6 (versioning and changelog). Missing indicators: 1 (periodic reassessment cadence is partially supported but explicit triggers/conditions are not), 2 (explicit assessment triggers), 3 (defined scope of assessments), 4 (adherence assessment including non-adherence causes), 7 (remediation planning). Alignment overreach treats indicator 1 as unmet due to lack of explicit triggers and explicit linkage to remediation; overall, the framework partially fulfills the requirement but does not fully address the core operational mechanisms.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioning with major/minor revisions
Version Control Table / changelog-like history
Living document with periodic updates (semi-annual cadence)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit assessment triggers and conditions for event-driven framework assessments are not defined.
Defined periodic reassessment cadence with clear intervals and the processes to conduct them are lacking.
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of adequacy relative to systemic risks of the models, is missing.
Framework adherence assessment mechanisms, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes, are missing.
Remediation planning criteria and processes for addressing identified risks of non-adherence or gaps are missing.
A formal mechanism showing how assessment findings drive updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art is not described (closure of the loop).

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The framework defines a versioning system, a changelog-like history, and a living-document update cadence (including semi-annual review), but does not clearly specify explicit assessment triggers, periodic reassessments, framework adequacy/adherence evaluation, or remediation planning.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: It aligns on versioning, change history, and a living-document approach with periodic updates, but lacks explicit criteria for assessment triggers, adequacy/adherence evaluation, and remediation planning.

Version Control Table / changelog-like history
Living document with periodic updates (semi-annual review)

evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows a defined cadence for updates, implying periodic review
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Indicator 1: Periodic reassessment / periodic review cadence

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The EU requirement asks for explicit triggers and processes for both periodic and event-driven framework assessments, including adequacy/adherence evaluation and remediation planning, which are not clearly defined in the retrieved text. The text mainly covers versioning, changelogs, and a living-document/update cadence, but lacks explicit assessment triggers, scope, and remediation mechanisms.
missing_elements: Explicit assessment triggers and conditions that prompt a framework assessment (event-driven triggers).
Defined periodic reassessment cadence with clearly stated intervals and the processes to conduct them.
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of framework adequacy relative to systemic risks of the models.
Framework adherence assessment, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
Remediation planning criteria and processes for addressing identified risks of non-adherence or framework gaps.
A formal mechanism showing how assessment findings drive updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art.
weaker_areas: Periodic reassessment cadence is implied by a semi-annual update cycle but lacks explicit, formal triggers or a clearly defined assessment process (i.e., event-driven reassessments).
The linkage between assessment findings and updates (closing the loop to maintain state-of-the-art) is not explicitly described.
scope_divergences: Divergence: EU requirement emphasizes explicit event-driven triggers and a defined assessment scope; the text centers on versioning, changelogs, and periodic updates without clearly defined assessment triggers or remediation planning.
Divergence: Absence of documented remediation planning and explicit consideration of non-adherence in framework assessments.
alignment_overreach: Indicator 1 claim of periodic reassessment/periodic review cadence is only partially supported by evidence of semi-annual updates and a living document; explicit assessment triggers and formal reassessment processes are not described.

results.title: AI Office notification
results.requirement: Acknowledge the obligation to notify the AI Office of the Safety and Security Framework and its updates, in line with Measure 1.4 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Measure 1.4 Framework notifications: Does the framework acknowledge the obligation to notify the AI Office of the framework and its updates, including any intended notification timing?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly acknowledges an obligation to notify or inform the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework.
The framework indicates that updates to the framework are also subject to notification.
The framework references the intended timing for such notification (e.g. after confirmation or update).
results.reasoning: None of the three Expected Evidence indicators are present: there is no explicit obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework, no requirement to notify about updates, and no defined timing for notifications. The text mentions only general feedback channels and versioning/update processes, which do not establish a formal notification mechanism or timing to the AI Office.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework or its updates; no defined timing for such notifications; only general feedback channels and versioning are described.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text does not acknowledge an obligation to notify the AI Office of the Safety and Security Framework or its updates, nor specify timing for such notification; it only describes general feedback channels and versioning/updates without reference to an AI Office notification requirement.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: No explicit alignment to the obligation to notify an AI Office is present; updates are described via versioning and feedback, but without a formal notification obligation to the AI Office or timing.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework does not acknowledge an obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework or its updates, nor specify any timing for such notifications. It only mentions general feedback channels and versioning, with no formal notification mechanism to the AI Office.
missing_elements: Explicit obligation to notify the AI Office about the Safety and Security Framework
Explicit obligation to notify the AI Office about updates to the Safety and Security Framework
Defined timing for notifications to the AI Office (e.g., after confirmation of changes or update release)
weaker_areas: Notification mechanism to AI Office missing; only general feedback channel exists without a formal notification obligation

and expected outcomes. NIST intends to work collaboratively with others to develop metrics, methodologies, and goals for evaluating the AI RMF’s effectiveness, and to broadly
share results and supporting information. Framework users are expected to benefit from:

• enhanced organizational culture which prioritizes the identification and management
of AI system risks and potential impacts to individuals, communities, organizations,
and society;

results.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
results.reasoning: None of the five Expected Evidence indicators are demonstrated in the retrieved text; the framework presents a general risk management lifecycle (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) without an explicit systemic risk identification process aligned to Appendix 1.1–1.4 or the enumeration of Appendix 1 risks. Alignment_overreach noted in the gap analysis confirms the claimed Appendix-1-informed identification is not supported.

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to

outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these

selected_evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and
others. Priority research and additional guidance that will enhance this Framework will be
captured in an associated AI Risk Management Framework Roadmap to which NIST and
the broader community can contribute.

Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The
first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

results.title: Model-independent information
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
results.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.
results.reasoning: Met: indicator 1 is supported by text showing systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information via external expert consultation and input from AI actors. Missing: indicators 2–4 are not clearly satisfied—the text does not define systematic breadth/depth controls, a full taxonomy of information-gathering methods, or an explicit description of how model-independent information informs downstream systemic risk analysis stages; alignment_overreach notes these gaps as unmet.
key_aligned_concepts: External expert consultation informs systemic risk analysis
Engagement with external AI actors feeds risk information into governance/management processes
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No systematic framework for model-independent information gathering with structured breadth and depth controls tied to risk characteristics

No full taxonomy of information-gathering methods (e.g., OSINT/web searches, literature reviews, market analyses, historical incident reviews, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews/panels, participatory/community-based research)
No explicit description of how breadth/depth is determined based on the characteristics or severity of systemic risk
No clear description of how model-independent information informs downstream systemic risk analysis stages (evaluations, modelling, or estimation) even if those stages have not yet been performed

a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors

established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.

Effectiveness of the AI RMF
Evaluations of AI RMF effectiveness – including ways to measure bottom-line improvements in the trustworthiness of AI systems – will be part of future NIST activities, in

Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,

Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the

occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,

results.title: Risk estimation
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the estimation of the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks, using at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods and taking into account relevant information inputs.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks are intended to be estimated using state-of-the-art methods, taking into account relevant information from systemic risk identification, analysis, and serious incident reporting, and how such estimates are expressed?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that probability and severity of harm are estimated as part of systemic risk analysis.
The framework indicates that at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods are used, appropriate to the systemic risk being assessed.

The framework explains that risk estimation takes into account relevant information inputs, such as outputs from systemic risk identification and analysis and information about serious incidents or near misses.

The framework describes how estimates of systemic risk are expressed, for example as risk scores, risk matrices, probability distributions, or other qualitative, semi-quantitative, or quantitative formats.
The framework explains the purpose of risk estimation in supporting systemic risk acceptance determination, without requiring specific numerical or qualitative results.
results.reasoning: The text presents only high-level risk framing (probability and harm) and generic risk measurement concepts but provides no operational description of estimating probability/severity of systemic risks using state-of-the-art methods, no inputs from systemic risk identification or incident reporting, no explicit formats for expressing estimates, and no stated link to systemic risk acceptance decisions. results.title: Post-market monitoring
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
results.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.
results.reasoning: Indicators 1, 2, 5, and 6 are evidenced in the retrieved text, demonstrating production-level post-market monitoring, risk-informed updates, and external evaluator safeguards. Indicators 3 (explicit enumeration of post-market monitoring methods) and 4 (Signatory-specific applicability/applicability to deployed AI systems) are not evidenced, and there is no explicit access to internal artifacts (model versions, chains-of-thought, safety-reduced variants) or vulnerability-disclosure timelines. These operational specifics cannot be substituted by thematic alignment alone.

Safeguards for external evaluators (selection criteria, information security, responsible disclosure, non-retaliation)

The framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers or, where tiers are not suitable and the risk is not a specified systemic risk, alternative acceptance criteria.

specific. Risk tolerances can be influenced by policies and norms established by AI system owners, organizations, industries, communities, or policy makers. Risk tolerances are
likely to change over time as AI systems, policies, and norms evolve. Different organizations may have varied risk tolerances due to their particular organizational priorities and
resource considerations.
Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may
be contexts where a risk management framework is not yet readily applicable for mitigating
negative AI risks.
The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations
should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and
response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional
requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or
established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and

established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and
use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should
define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

All involved AI actors share responsibilities for designing, developing, and deploying a
trustworthy AI system that is fit for purpose.

environment may yield important insights pre-deployment, these measurements may differ
from risks that emerge in operational, real-world settings.
Inscrutability: Inscrutable AI systems can complicate risk measurement. Inscrutability
can be a result of the opaque nature of AI systems (limited explainability or interpretability), lack of transparency or documentation in AI system development or deployment, or
inherent uncertainties in AI systems.
Human baseline: Risk management of AI systems that are intended to augment or replace
human activity, for example decision making, requires some form of baseline metrics for
comparison. This is difficult to systematize since AI systems carry out different tasks – and
perform tasks differently – than humans.

resources.

results.title: Proceeding decisions
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines decisions to proceed with, restrict, or not proceed with the development, making available on the market, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how decisions to proceed or not proceed with the development, market availability, or use of the model are made based on systemic risk acceptance determination, and how responses are defined when risks are not acceptable or are likely to become unacceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework states that proceeding with development, making available on the market, or use of the model is conditional on systemic risks being determined acceptable.
The framework states that if systemic risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable, appropriate measures must be taken before proceeding.
The framework describes possible actions when risks are not acceptable, such as not making the model available on the market, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model.
The framework states that safety and/or security mitigations are to be implemented when systemic risks are not acceptable.

The framework states that another round of systemic risk identification, systemic risk analysis, and systemic risk acceptance determination is to be conducted when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable.
results.reasoning: All five Expected Evidence indicators are unmet. The text discusses risk tolerance and governance but does not provide explicit decision criteria for proceeding/not proceeding with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance, nor defined responses, mitigations, or re-approval cycles; alignment overreach confirms this gap.
key_aligned_concepts: Risk tolerance governance
Regulatory and sector-aligned risk management
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit decision criteria tied to systemic risk acceptance for proceeding with development, market availability, or use (SS-4.2).

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.

– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

results.title: Safety mitigations
results.requirement: The framework defines and requires the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define and require the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework describes categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks.
The framework explains that safety mitigations are designed to be robust under adversarial pressure, such as attempts to bypass or subvert them.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations take into account the model's release and distribution strategy.
The framework provides examples of safety mitigation approaches, such as e.g. input or output filtering, behaviour modification, staged access, or other emerging safety techniques.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations are considered and adapted across the model lifecycle.

segments.
Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.
3.2
Safe
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

expected_evidence: The framework explicitly links security mitigations to achieving a defined Security Goal.

The framework indicates that security mitigations align with the mitigation objectives defined in Appendix 4, such as general security protections, protection of unreleased model parameters, interface-access hardening, insider threat mitigation, and security assurance.

The framework indicates that specific security measures may vary depending on organisational context or infrastructure, and explains how alternative mitigations achieve equivalent mitigation objectives.
The framework indicates that security mitigations may be implemented in stages as model capabilities increase along the model lifecycle.
results.reasoning: None of the five Expected Evidence indicators are explicitly present in the text: no explicit link between security mitigations and a defined Security Goal, no mapping to Appendix 4 objectives or equivalent measures, no description of alternative mitigations, and no explicit staged implementation plan across the model lifecycle. evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases and potential conflicts of interest.
Where tradeoffs among the trustworthy characteristics arise, measurement provides a traceable basis to inform management decisions. Options may include recalibration, impact
mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodologies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and transparent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

is acceptable to organizations or society are highly contextual and application and use-case

Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may

results.requirement: Describe in the Model Report how the systemic risk framework has been applied to the model, including reported results of systemic risk identification, analysis, modelling, estimation, evaluations, implemented safety and security mitigations, their limitations, and planned future developments.
results.assessment_question: What must the Model Report document regarding systemic risk identification, modelling, and estimates, including model evaluation results with random input/output samples, comparisons between safety-mitigated and fully elicited model versions, independent external evaluator access, Security Goal and mitigation limitations, and planned future model capabilities over the next six months?
expected_evidence: The Model Report describes the reported results of systemic risk identification and analysis, including assumptions, uncertainties, and links to the risk types defined in the framework.
The Model Report explains the reported outcomes of systemic risk modelling and estimation, including how risks are characterised and compared with and without mitigations.
The Model Report summarises relevant model evaluation approaches and results used to understand systemic risks, including illustrative examples or references.
The Model Report describes implemented safety mitigations and their limitations, and explains how they align with the framework’s safety requirements.
The Model Report describes the Security Goal and implemented security mitigations, including alignment with defined mitigation objectives or justified alternatives.
The Model Report includes a high-level forward-looking description of planned model developments and anticipated changes to capabilities, risks, and mitigations.
results.reasoning: The Model Report covers systemic risk identification, mapping, and evaluation (MAP 4/5; TEVV/MEASURE) and forward-looking versioning, but it misses explicit random input/output sampling, independent external evaluator access, direct comparative analyses between safety-mitigated and fully elicited versions, a six-month horizon, explicit assumptions/uncertainties linked to risk types, and a defined Security Goal with aligned mitigations.

Risk at different stages of the AI lifecycle: Measuring risk at an earlier stage in the AI

be latent at a given point in time and may increase as AI systems adapt and evolve. Furthermore, different AI actors across the AI lifecycle can have different risk perspectives.

results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines obligations to update the Model Report when the justification for systemic risk acceptability is materially undermined, and whether it specifies periodic update expectations, versioning, and changelog requirements in line with Measure 7.6.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe when Model Report updates are required, including material undermining triggers, timing expectations, periodic updates for most capable models, and versioning/changelog requirements?
expected_evidence: The framework describes circumstances under which the justification for systemic risk acceptability may be materially undermined and requires a Model Report update in such cases.
The framework lists or references example triggers for updates, such as material changes in model capabilities, use, integrations, serious incidents, or evaluation validity.
The framework specifies expectations regarding the timing of Model Report updates, including completion within a reasonable time and prior to market release for deliberate changes.
The framework acknowledges periodic Model Report updates for the most capable models (e.g. at least every six months), including applicable exemptions.
The framework requires updated Model Reports to include versioning information and a changelog explaining how and why updates were made.

the goal of the AI RMF is to offer a resource to the organizations designing, developing,
deploying, or using AI systems to help manage the many risks of AI and promote trustworthy and responsible development and use of AI systems. The Framework is intended to be

foster the responsible design, development, deployment, and use of AI systems over time.

The AI RMF is intended to be practical, to adapt to the AI landscape as AI technologies
continue to develop, and to be operationalized by organizations in varying degrees and
capacities so society can benefit from AI while also being protected from its potential
harms.

results.title: Responsibilities
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines clear responsibilities for managing systemic risks, including systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance, and how these responsibilities are allocated across organisational governance levels.
results.assessment_question: How must signatories assign systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance responsibilities across the management body in its supervisory and executive functions, operational teams, and internal and external assurance providers, including role-specific requirements such as separation from core business activities and cascading responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly defines responsibilities for systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance.
The framework describes how systemic risk oversight is assigned to a supervisory or otherwise independent governance function.
The framework describes how systemic risk ownership is assigned to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk support and monitoring is assigned to functions that are organisationally independent from core business activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk assurance is provided to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and, where applicable, external assurance.
The framework acknowledges proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity (e.g. SMEs or SMCs).
results.reasoning: Evidence shows executive-level ownership and cross-cutting governance support (GOVERN 2.3; GOVERN 1.5; GOVERN 2.1) but it lacks explicit independent supervisory/oversight structures, formal systemic risk assurance, SME/SMC-based proportional allocation, and clear separation from core business with governance-level mapping. Alignment_overreach flags these missing structural indicators, which cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Documented roles and responsibilities for AI risk management
Executive leadership accountability for AI risk decisions
Ongoing monitoring and defined responsibilities
Governance as an integrated, cross-cutting function
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit independent supervisory or governance function for systemic risk oversight separate from core business activities
Formal systemic risk assurance arrangements to a supervisory or independent body (internal and external) with defined responsibilities and timelines
Proportional allocation of systemic risk responsibilities based on organizational size and complexity (e.g., SMEs/SMCs)
Clear separation of roles between risk-producing activities and oversight/support activities
Explicit mapping of systemic risk oversight, ownership, support/monitoring, and assurance across distinct governance levels (board, management, risk bodies) with defined authorities

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text partially addresses the EU code's requirement by documenting governance roles and ownership for AI risk management (including executive responsibility and ongoing monitoring) but it does not explicitly define independent supervisory/assurance structures or proportional SME/SMC allocation.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework establishes clear governance roles, executive risk ownership, and ongoing monitoring, aligning with the EU requirement's governance-level responsibilities. However, it lacks explicit references to independent oversight/assurance, separation from core business, and SME/SMC proportional allocation.

Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms,
roles and responsibilities, culture, and incentive structures for risk management to be effective. Use of the AI RMF alone will not lead to these changes or provide the appropriate
incentives. Effective risk management is realized through organizational commitment at
senior levels and may require cultural change within an organization or industry. In addition, small to medium-sized organizations managing AI risks or implementing the AI RMF
may face different challenges than large organizations, depending on their capabilities and
resources.

represent a diversity of experience, expertise, and backgrounds and comprise demographically and disciplinarily diverse teams. The AI RMF is intended to be used by AI actors
across the AI lifecycle and dimensions.

GOVERN is a cross-cutting function that is infused throughout AI risk management and
enables the other functions of the process. Aspects of GOVERN, especially those related to
compliance or evaluation, should be integrated into each of the other functions. Attention
to governance is a continual and intrinsic requirement for effective AI risk management
over an AI system’s lifespan and the organization’s hierarchy.
Strong governance can drive and enhance internal practices and norms to facilitate organizational risk culture. Governing authorities can determine the overarching policies that
direct an organization’s mission, goals, values, culture, and risk tolerance. Senior leadership sets the tone for risk management within an organization, and with it, organizational
culture. Management aligns the technical aspects of AI risk management to policies and
operations. Documentation can enhance transparency, improve human review processes,
and bolster accountability in AI system teams.
After putting in place the structures, systems, processes, and teams described in the GOVERN function, organizations should benefit from a purpose-driven culture focused on risk

and documented.

Subcategories
5.4
Manage
The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.
After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring
and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

results.title: Resources
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework specifies that management bodies oversee the allocation of resources appropriate to the systemic risks, for actors assigned systemic risk responsibilities.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework explicitly acknowledge management oversight of resource allocation for systemic risk responsibilities and specify the categories of resources to be considered?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly states that management bodies oversee the allocation of resources for managing systemic risks.
The framework links resource allocation to the responsibilities defined for systemic risk management.
The framework specifies that resource allocation must be appropriate to the systemic risks stemming from the model.
The framework explicitly identifies human resources as a required resource category for systemic risk management.
The framework explicitly identifies financial resources as a required resource category for systemic risk management.
The framework explicitly identifies access to information and knowledge as a required resource category for systemic risk management.
The framework explicitly identifies computational resources as a required resource category for systemic risk management.
results.reasoning: The framework partially meets the indicators: it links resource allocation to risk priorities and governance, and notes resources are allocated according to organizational risk priorities, but it does not explicitly state management bodies oversee the allocation nor enumerate required resource categories (human, financial, information/knowledge, computational).
key_aligned_concepts: Resource allocation linked to risk priorities
Governance-guided risk management (MANAGE/GOV functions)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit management body oversight of resource allocation for systemic risks is absent.
No enumeration of required resource categories: human, financial, information/knowledge, computational.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No—the framework links resource allocation to assessed risk priorities and governance but does not explicitly state that management bodies oversee allocation or enumerate the required resource categories (human, financial, information/knowledge, computational).
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework conceptually ties resource allocation to governance-defined risk priorities, but it does not explicitly confirm management body oversight or enumerate specific resource categories as required.

results.title: Risk culture
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework promotes a healthy systemic risk culture, including leadership tone, openness to challenge, independence of systemic risk functions, and protections for reporting and whistleblowing.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework explicitly acknowledge the importance of a healthy systemic risk culture and describe principles or mechanisms intended to promote it?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the importance of promoting a healthy systemic risk culture.
The framework describes leadership responsibilities or tone-from-the-top communication regarding systemic risk.
The framework states that challenge, escalation, or critical discussion of systemic risk decisions is encouraged.
The framework describes independence or safeguards for actors involved in systemic risk assessment and mitigation.
The framework references internal reporting or whistleblowing channels related to systemic risks.
The framework includes a non-retaliation commitment or protection for individuals raising systemic risk concerns.
results.reasoning: Indicator 1 is present (explicit recognition of a healthy risk culture). Indicators 2–6 (leadership tone-from-the-top, escalation/challenge mechanisms, independence safeguards, internal reporting/whistleblowing channels, and non-retaliation protections) are missing; their binary operational nature cannot be offset by thematic alignment, resulting in a failure to fully meet the EU requirement.
key_aligned_concepts: Enhanced organizational culture prioritizing AI risk identification and management
Engagement with interested parties and information sharing to strengthen risk culture
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit leadership tone-from-the-top responsibilities or communication regarding systemic risk
Clear challenge, escalation, or critical discussion mechanisms for systemic risk decisions
Independence safeguards or protections for actors involved in systemic risk assessment and mitigation
References to internal reporting or whistleblowing channels related to systemic risks
Non-retaliation commitments or protections for individuals raising systemic risk concerns

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes — the AI Risk Management Framework explicitly references an enhanced organizational culture prioritizing the identification and management of AI system risks and related engagement/information-sharing mechanisms to promote a healthy risk culture.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text acknowledges the importance of a healthy risk culture and describes cultural enhancements and stakeholder engagement as mechanisms to promote it; however, explicit leadership tone, challenge/escalation practices, independence safeguards, whistleblowing protections, or reporting channels are not detailed in the provided excerpt.

evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework explicitly recognises the importance of promoting a healthy systemic risk culture.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework partially recognizes a healthy AI/systemic risk culture but omits explicit leadership tone, challenge/escalation mechanics, independence safeguards, internal reporting/whistleblowing channels, and non-retaliation protections as required by the EU requirement.

Clear challenge, escalation, or critical discussion mechanisms for systemic risk decisions

results.title: Incident identification
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines methods and channels for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle, including consideration of external sources and facilitation of third-party reporting.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe approaches for identifying serious incidents, including monitoring external sources and enabling third-party reporting?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the need to identify and track serious incidents across the model lifecycle.
The framework describes intended methods for identifying serious incidents, including reference to post-market monitoring or similar processes.
The framework references consideration of external information sources (e.g. media, incident databases, research, public reporting).
The framework describes how downstream providers, users, or other third parties may report serious incidents to the Signatory and/or authorities.
results.reasoning: None of the four Expected Evidence indicators are explicitly present: explicit lifecycle-wide methods for identifying/tracking serious incidents, post-market monitoring, consideration of external information sources, and defined third-party reporting channels are not described. Alignment shows only conceptual lifecycle risk management and general third-party monitoring, which cannot compensate for the missing operational requirements; alignment_overreach is noted as such.
key_aligned_concepts: Incident identification and response within lifecycle risk management (conceptual alignment under MANAGE 2.3).
Lifecycle coverage of AI risk management functions (MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) across stages of the AI lifecycle.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit lifecycle-wide methods for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the AI lifecycle are absent.
Post-market monitoring or equivalent ongoing mechanisms for detecting incidents after deployment are not described.
External information sources (e.g., media, incident databases, research, public reporting) are not explicitly considered as inputs for incident identification.
Defined channels and procedures for third-party reporting of serious incidents to the Signatory and/or authorities, including recipients and timelines, are missing.
Defined retention, notification, escalation, and remediation timelines related to incident reporting and tracking are not described.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The framework references lifecycle-oriented risk management and incident response concepts (including monitoring third-party resources and responding to identified risks) but does not explicitly describe methods, post-market monitoring, external information sources, or reporting channels for serious incidents across the lifecycle.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework conceptually supports incident identification and lifecycle risk management and notes third-party monitoring, but it lacks explicit detailing of post-market monitoring, external sources, and third-party reporting channels required by the EU criterion.
key_aligned_concepts: Incident identification and response within lifecycle risk management (conceptual alignment under MANAGE 2.3).
Lifecycle coverage of AI risk management functions (MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) across stages of the AI lifecycle.

results.title: Incident documentation
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
results.reasoning: None of the five Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text: explicit minimum information categories for serious incidents, mandatory root cause analysis (including model inputs/outputs and risk-mitigation failures), guidance on using post-market monitoring signals, explicit handling of missing information, and a principle that detail scales with incident severity. As operational, binary requirements are absent, thematic alignment cannot compensate to meet the criterion.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit minimum information categories for serious incidents (e.g., timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, response actions).
No requirement for root cause analysis (including examination of model outputs/inputs and failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations).
No guidance on how post-market monitoring signals inform incident analysis.
No explicit handling/recording of information unavailable at reporting time.
No principle that the level of detail is proportionate to the incident severity.
